analysis.title: What are the biggest market dislocations? November 2026
key_insights: DB (Henry Allen) says bonds and equities are pricing different macro regimes and stress is growing: the S&P 500 closed at a 6-week low last Friday, US and European credit spreads widened in October, and the 2yr Treasury yield had its biggest monthly decline in over a year.

The current equilibrium implies a very narrow landing zone. If growth keeps weakening and stress spreads, equities will struggle to stay immune to credit weakness. If growth is resilient, demand-side inflation continues, pushing yields higher and raising the risk of faster rate hikes.

Dislocation 1: the Jan 2027 Brent contract rose 19% in October to $113/bbl and near-term inflation swaps rose (Euro 1yr +27bps to 3.86%, US 1yr +14bps to 2.63%), yet the Fed rate priced for June 2027 fell 30bps and the ECB rate priced for June 2027 fell 22bps.

DB argues that central banks are historically constrained from a dovish pivot when inflation is above target, and financial conditions remain accommodative in aggregate. Investors may be underestimating central bank hawkishness. The report cites the 2022-23 cycle, when banks kept hiking after the SVB collapse.

Dislocation 2: the oil futures curve keeps pricing a normalisation in prices that has not happened, and longer-term inflation expectations have barely moved. The 5yr Euro inflation swap closed at 2.46% versus 2.43% at the start of the month and a 2.54% April peak. Markets are not pricing second-round effects.

DB says the low long-term inflation expectations are hard to explain by tighter policy, since markets priced looser policy in October, or by demand destruction, since longer-dated oil futures also rose. The risk is that persistence of inflation and second-round effects is underestimated.

Dislocation 3: credit stress is not matched in equities. US HY spreads hit 340bps, the widest since May 2025, and US IG spreads hit 90bps, the highest since March. The S&P 500 is only 3% below its record, the VIX has not closed above 20 in over 3 months, and the STOXX 600 is 2% below its record.

In prior episodes with similarly wide spreads, the S&P 500 was down over 9% from its peak (March 2026, IG spreads) and almost 8% (May 2025, HY spreads). Wider spreads raise the cost of capital and tighten financial conditions, which can feed back into equities.

Dislocation 4: the STOXX 600 rose 1.9% in local currency in October, while European HY spreads widened 65bps (biggest monthly widening since 2022) and the Euro fell 1.5% against the USD, the worst G10 currency. The Franco-German 10yr spread is near its widest since the early 2010s Euro crisis.

Dislocation 5: the three main risks (oil from geopolitics, French-centred fiscal concerns, AI growth concerns hitting tech) partly offset each other. AI weakness would lower yields and ease fiscal worries, reduce oil and memory chip demand and make rate hikes less likely. Tighter financial conditions also do part of the work of rate hikes.

The offsets have limits: if growth slows meaningfully, equities lose support even if yields and oil fall, and if growth holds up, central banks face hawkish pressure over the energy shock. DB says the biggest dislocation may be how compartmentalised the risks still are, and the question is whether they stay contained.

sector_views.rationale: Tech struggled globally in October on AI-driven growth concerns. Europe's smaller tech exposure partly explains the STOXX 600's outperformance.

tension_points.bull_case: Equities are holding up, with the S&P 500 3% below its record, the VIX under 20 for over 3 months and the STOXX 600 2% below its record. Risks offset each other: AI weakness lowers yields and eases fiscal worries, and tighter financial conditions reduce the need for rate hikes.
tension_points.bear_case: Credit spreads are at their widest in over a year (US HY 340bps) and wider spreads tighten financial conditions and hurt growth, which can pull equities lower. In earlier episodes with similar spreads the S&P 500 was down 8-9%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A meaningful growth slowdown would remove equity support even if yields and oil fall, and resilient growth would keep hawkish pressure on central banks.

tension_points.bull_case: Markets price looser policy, with the Fed's June 2027 rate down 30bps, and long-term inflation expectations contained (5yr Euro swap 2.46%).
tension_points.bear_case: Oil is up 19% in a month and the shock is persisting, so second-round effects and central bank hawkishness may be underestimated.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Second-round effects appearing in other sectors' pricing, which DB says often take several months after the initial shock.

theme_stances.key_argument: Credit spreads have widened to levels that previously came with larger equity drawdowns, yet equities remain near record highs.
Markets have priced out rate hikes despite higher oil and near-term inflation, so central bank hawkishness may be underestimated.
theme_stances.evidence: investors are underestimating central bank hawkishness
